entries.title: The Brennan's Turtle Soup
entries.summary: Brennan's signature soup at breakfast, lunch and dinner: a dark, roux-thickened Creole soup of 100 per cent turtle meat, built on the trinity and a rich stock, finished with aged sherry, brown butter spinach and grated egg.
entries.guest: Our Turtle Soup is a Brennan's classic: 100 per cent turtle meat in a rich, dark Creole soup, with brown butter spinach, grated egg and a splash of aged sherry.

paras: Turtle soup is the bowl that tells a guest what Brennan's is about: a dark, thick Creole soup, long cooked, served at breakfast, lunch and dinner and as the second course of the Traditional Breakfast. For many guests it is the first turtle they have eaten, so say the word plainly and describe the taste rather than the animal: rich, meaty and savoury, like a deep, finely chopped stew.

The menu prints 100 per cent turtle meat, and the words matter. Many turtle soups, in restaurants and in cans, are stretched with veal or beef, and mock turtle has no turtle at all. Ours is all turtle: dark, firm meat full of gelatine, somewhere between veal and dark chicken, and that gelatine, with the roux, gives the soup its body.

This is the Creole build, taught step by step in Creole turtle soup; how our kitchen does each step, and how dark it takes the roux, is a chef question. A brown roux, flour cooked in fat to the colour of milk chocolate until it smells of toasted nuts, meets the trinity of onion, celery and green pepper; tomato, a rich brown stock and finely chopped turtle follow, the stock a ladle at a time, and the soup simmers gently, skimmed, until it coats a spoon.

Roux and stock meet at different temperatures, never both hot, so the flour disperses before it swells. The classic proportion is about 115 g (4 oz) each of fat and flour to 2 litres (about 2 quarts) of stock, more than a pale sauce would need, since a brown roux thickens less. The turtle needs a long, gentle simmer, often well over an hour, until it is tender; the soup then takes a further 45 minutes to an hour at a lazy bubble, about 90°C (194°F), to cook out the flour and bring the flavours together. How our kitchen times it is a chef question.

The finish comes last. Lemon juice brightens it, hard-boiled egg enriches it, spinach brings colour and an earthy note, and dry, aged sherry cuts the richness the way lemon lifts fish. Hold the finished soup at 57°C (135°F) or above, the FDA Food Code figure for hot holding.

A turtle soup fails in the roux and in the simmer. A roux with black flecks or an acrid smell makes the whole pot bitter, and no seasoning hides it: start again. Hot stock poured all at once into a hot roux turns lumpy. A hard boil makes the soup greasy and the meat stringy. A dark soup that stays thin needs more roux, and a flat one wants salt, lemon or the sherry.

At Brennan's the soup is made with snapping turtle, a freshwater turtle, by the house guide's account, chopped finely and simmered long so it spreads through the soup. Louisiana closed the wild alligator snapper to commercial trappers, so restaurants buy from licensed farms or collectors; whether ours is farm-raised, and from whom, is a question for the chef, confirmed at lineup, the short staff meeting before each service, before you name anyone.

Spinach wilted in brown butter, nutty and soft, is folded through, and hard-boiled egg is grated over the top; the body comes from the roux and the gelatine, not the egg. Aged sherry finishes it, and whether it goes in at the stove, at the pass (the counter where plates leave the kitchen) or at the table is a lineup question.

Builders found turtles in the courtyard during the 2014 restoration, and the house adopted them. Ten live there now, named for sauces: five for the French mother sauces as kitchens teach them, from béchamel to hollandaise, and five for New Orleans sauces. Say it before a guest asks, with a smile: the soup is not the turtles.

Offer the soup to every first visit and to anyone who asks what New Orleans tastes like. Sherry is in the bowl, so tell a guest avoiding alcohol before they order, and never promise that it cooks off. The soup carries egg, butter in the spinach and, in the Creole tradition, a wheat flour roux, so every allergen question goes to the service note and the kitchen. On the Traditional Breakfast the guest chooses this or the Seafood Gumbo, and either comes with a Bloody Bull, a Bloody Mary made with beef bouillon: both are soups, so read the ticket twice.

entries.title: The Brennan's Seafood Gumbo
entries.summary: Brennan's signature gumbo: shrimp, crab and oysters with smoky andouille, simmered into a dark-roux Creole seafood gumbo over Louisiana popcorn rice, served at breakfast, lunch and dinner and as a soup choice on the Traditional Breakfast.
entries.guest: Our Seafood Gumbo is shrimp, crab and oysters with smoky andouille sausage, over Louisiana popcorn rice: savoury, briny and smoky, with gentle spice.

paras: Gumbo, GUM-boh, is the dish that says Louisiana: a dark stew usually built on a roux and served with rice. Its name most likely comes from a West African word for okra, its roux from French cooking taken darker in Louisiana, and its filé, ground sassafras leaves, from the Choctaw. Roux is one of three thickeners: okra, simmered, gives a silky body, and filé is stirred in off the heat or at the table, because boiling turns it stringy. Many gumbos use a roux with one of the others, and some use okra or filé alone. A seafood gumbo stands on a stock made from the shells, and the seafood goes in at the very end.

Ours is a Brennan's signature at breakfast, lunch and dinner: shrimp, crab and oysters with smoky andouille, over Louisiana popcorn rice, and the alternative to the turtle soup on the Traditional Breakfast. It tastes savoury, briny and smoky, with gentle spice: sweetness from the seafood, smoke and warmth from the sausage.

The full technique belongs to Seafood gumbo; here is the order of the build. First a stock from the shrimp shells and crab bodies, kept short so it never turns bitter; then a dark roux of flour and oil, stirred to the colour of dark chocolate; then the trinity of onion, celery and green pepper, which stops the roux browning, with garlic, the browned andouille and the stock, a ladle at a time; then a gentle simmer, skimmed. The seafood goes in last, by the time each needs: FDA guidance cooks seafood to 63°C (145°F), when shrimp turn pearly and opaque and oysters plump, while the picked crab, already cooked, is only heated through.

Most gumbo faults start in the roux. Black flecks or an acrid smell mean it burnt, and the gumbo will taste bitter: start again. A dark gumbo that stays thin needs more roux, because a dark roux thickens less; a pasty, muddy one had too much, or too short a simmer to cook out the flour. A greasy surface was never skimmed. Rubbery shrimp and shrunken oysters were cooked too long or held in the pot, and a harsh stock sat too long on its shells.

The menu prints shrimp, crab, oysters, andouille and popcorn rice, and names no source for the seafood, so where today's comes from is a kitchen question. Gulf shrimp, brown or white by season, want only a couple of minutes. Picked lump crab is sweet and already cooked, so it is only warmed. Gulf oysters are large and mild from brackish water. Andouille is a coarse, heavily smoked pork sausage, made to season a pot rather than to eat alone. Popcorn rice is a Louisiana aromatic long grain that smells of popcorn as it cooks and keeps its grains firm and separate in the broth.

Brennan's published gumbo recipe starts from a dark mahogany roux with andouille and okra in crab stock, and carries tomato and filé, but the menu prints none of those, so never promise them: say published recipe, never menu, and only once the chef confirms at lineup, the short staff meeting before each service, that the dining room gumbo follows it.

Suggest the gumbo to seafood lovers, to a guest who wants something hearty before an egg dish, and to anyone choosing a soup on the Traditional Breakfast, where either soup comes with a Bloody Bull, a Bloody Mary made with beef bouillon. The spice is mild to moderate. Every spoonful carries shrimp, crab and oysters, the andouille is pork and gumbo is usually built on a wheat flour roux, so every allergen or diet question goes to the service note and the kitchen before the guest orders. A toasty smell as the bowl lands is the rice.

Gumbo joins West African okra and its name, a French roux and Choctaw filé; ours is a Creole seafood gumbo, a signature at both meals and on the Traditional Breakfast.

cards.back: A West African word for okra. Its thickeners are a roux from French cooking, okra itself, and filé, ground sassafras from the Choctaw, stirred in off the heat because boiling turns it stringy.

entries.title: Redfish Véronique
entries.summary: The dinner menu's French classic with a Gulf fish: redfish with hibiscus-pickled grapes, braised leeks, fingerling potatoes and a preserved lemon beurre blanc. It is Brennan's take on Sole Véronique and the third course of the dinner tasting.
entries.guest: Our Redfish Véronique is the French classic of fish with grapes: redfish with hibiscus-pickled grapes, braised leeks, fingerling potatoes and a preserved lemon beurre blanc.

paras: À la Véronique, vay-ro-NEEK, means served with grapes. The classic is Sole Véronique: poached sole in a creamy white wine sauce with peeled green muscat grapes, glazed under the grill. Tradition credits it to Escoffier and names it for André Messager's operetta Véronique, first staged in Paris in 1898, but the chef and the date vary between tellings, so tell it as a story rather than a fact.

Brennan's keeps the idea and makes three changes: redfish for sole, a preserved lemon beurre blanc for the creamy sauce, and grapes pickled with hibiscus for fresh ones, over braised leeks and fingerling potatoes. It is a dinner main course and the third course of the dinner tasting, and it teaches three foundations at once: cooking a fillet, mounting a butter sauce and balancing acid.

Redfish, the red drum, has firm, mild, slightly sweet white flesh that holds together in a hot pan. A firm fillet like this is usually sautéed or pan-roasted: the pan and a little fat hot, the presentation side down first and left alone to colour, turned once and finished gently, in the oven if thick. FDA guidance cooks fish to 63°C (145°F), when the flesh turns opaque and flakes at a touch. How our kitchen cooks it is learned at lineup, the short staff meeting before each service.

A beurre blanc, burr BLAHN, starts as a reduction: about 100 ml (about 7 tbsp) of white wine and 50 ml (about 3 tbsp) of white wine vinegar with a finely chopped shallot, reduced to roughly 30 ml (2 tbsp). Over low heat, about 225 g (8 oz) of cold, diced butter is whisked in a few pieces at a time, so it softens into a creamy emulsion rather than melting into oil. Finely chopped preserved lemon rind, salty and perfumed, goes in at the end.

The sauce is held warm, about 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F), off direct heat: much hotter and the butter oils out, much cooler and it sets. The low end sits below 57°C (135°F), the FDA Food Code line for hot holding, so the kitchen makes it in small batches and replaces it on a schedule the chef sets rather than holding it all service.

Pickled grapes are steeped in a sweet and sour brine; a common kitchen method pours hot vinegar, water and sugar over halved grapes, and dried hibiscus in the brine turns them ruby and adds a tart, cranberry-like note. The balance is the lesson: butter and leek bring richness and sweetness, preserved lemon brings salt and perfume, the grapes bring sharpness and fruit. Taste the sauce and a grape together before the plate goes.

A beurre blanc fails by heat. Too hot, and the butter oils out into a greasy, separated sauce; too cool, and it sets thick and waxy. A sauce that is only starting to split can often be brought back off the heat by whisking it, a little at a time, into a spoonful of fresh reduction or cold cream in a clean pan. The fish fails by time: well past 63°C (145°F), redfish dries and tightens. The plate fails by balance: season the sauce after the preserved lemon goes in, never before, or it ends up salty.

On our plate: redfish, a firm, mild fish that lets the grapes and sauce speak; hibiscus-pickled grapes, sweet, tart and floral, in place of fresh muscat; braised leeks, soft and gently sweet, and fingerling potatoes, small and waxy, as the quiet base; and a preserved lemon beurre blanc. Where our redfish comes from is a question for the chef. Louisiana has barred the commercial catch of wild redfish since the late 1980s, after the blackened redfish craze, so restaurant redfish is farmed or comes from other sources.

Offer it to a guest who wants fish at dinner, something elegant and light, or a French classic with a local fish. If a guest is wary of fruit with fish, describe the grapes as a sharp relish rather than a sweet garnish. The plate is fish in a butter sauce, so every allergen question goes to the service note and the kitchen. On the dinner tasting the course is paired with a light red Burgundy, the printed Beaune Premier Cru; confirm the open bottle at lineup, and be ready to say why a light, low-tannin red suits the hibiscus grapes.

faults.fix: Off the heat, whisk it a little at a time into a spoonful of fresh reduction or cold cream in a clean pan.

faults.fix: Warm it gently over low heat, whisking, back to about 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F).
Pull it when the centre has just lost its translucence, a degree or two short of 63°C (145°F); carryover heat finishes it.

faults.fix: Add the lemon rind first, taste, then salt.

brennans.how: À la Véronique means with grapes; ours puts redfish, the red drum, where the classic has sole. Where our redfish comes from, farmed or another state's catch, is a question for the chef.
Cold butter mounted into a wine, vinegar and shallot reduction, brightened with preserved lemon, salty and perfumed; it replaces the creamy glazed sauce of Sole Véronique.
Grapes steeped in a sweet and sour brine with hibiscus, ruby, tart and floral, stand in for fresh muscat grapes; describe them to a wary guest as a sharp relish.
Leeks braised slowly in butter and stock until silky, with small waxy fingerling potatoes, make the gentle base under the fish, grapes and sauce.

cards.front: What does à la Véronique mean on a menu?
cards.back: Served with grapes, after Sole Véronique: poached sole in a creamy sauce with peeled muscat grapes, glazed under the grill. Say vay-ro-NEEK.

cards.front: By tradition, what is Sole Véronique named after?
cards.back: André Messager's operetta Véronique, first staged in Paris in 1898; tradition credits the dish to Escoffier, but tellings vary.

cards.front: What three changes does Brennan's make to Sole Véronique?
cards.back: Redfish for sole, a preserved lemon beurre blanc for the creamy sauce, and hibiscus-pickled grapes for fresh ones.

cards.front: What is redfish like, and why does it suit this dish?
cards.back: Red drum: firm, mild and slightly sweet, it holds together in the pan and lets the grapes and butter sauce speak.

cards.front: How is a beurre blanc made?
cards.back: Cold diced butter whisked a few pieces at a time into a reduction of white wine, vinegar and shallot over low heat, with no egg yolks.

cards.front: At what temperature is a beurre blanc held, and why?
cards.back: Warm, about 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F), off direct heat: much hotter the butter oils out, much cooler it sets. Below 57°C (135°F) it is made in small batches and replaced on the chef's schedule.

cards.front: What does preserved lemon bring to the sauce?
cards.back: Lemon cured in salt and its own juice: the rind brings a salty, perfumed lemon note rather than sharp sourness.

cards.front: What are hibiscus-pickled grapes?
cards.back: Grapes steeped in a sweet and sour brine with dried hibiscus: ruby, tart and floral, like a sharp relish against rich fish.

cards.front: How do you know the redfish is done?
cards.back: At 63°C (145°F) in the centre the flesh turns opaque and flakes at a touch; well past that it dries and tightens.

cards.front: Why is the source of our redfish a question for the chef?
cards.back: Louisiana closed its commercial redfish fishery in the late 1980s, so restaurant redfish is farmed or legally caught elsewhere.

cards.front: Which wine meets the Véronique on the dinner tasting?
cards.back: A light red Burgundy, the printed Beaune Premier Cru, whose red fruit meets the hibiscus grapes; confirm the open bottle at lineup.

cards.front: What sits beneath the fish on the Redfish Véronique?
cards.back: Braised leeks, soft and gently sweet, and fingerling potatoes, small and waxy: the quiet base under the bright grapes and sauce.

questions.q: What does à la Véronique tell a guest about a dish?
questions.answer: It is served with grapes
distractors: It is cooked in a paper parcel
It is finished with almonds
It is blackened in a hot pan
questions.why: Véronique is the classical name for a dish garnished with grapes, after Sole Véronique; en papillote, amandine (with almonds) and blackened are other dishes.

questions.q: Which of these is one of Brennan's three changes to Sole Véronique?
questions.answer: Hibiscus-pickled grapes for fresh ones
distractors: Pompano for the sole
A béarnaise in place of the cream sauce
Raisins for the fresh grapes
questions.why: The three changes are redfish for sole, a preserved lemon beurre blanc for the creamy sauce, and hibiscus-pickled grapes for fresh muscat.

questions.q: What does preserved lemon rind bring to the Véronique's beurre blanc?
questions.answer: A salty, perfumed lemon note
distractors: A sharp, sour bite like fresh juice
Sweetness to balance the grapes
A bitter edge like grapefruit pith
questions.why: Lemon cured in salt and its own juice loses its sharp bitterness; the chopped rind brings salt and a floral perfume rather than sourness.

questions.q: A beurre blanc at the pass has turned greasy and separated. What most likely went wrong?
questions.answer: It was held well above 60°C (140°F)
distractors: It needed more vinegar
The butter went in straight from the fridge
It was held too cool and set
questions.why: Beurre blanc holds at about 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F); much hotter and the butterfat melts out of the emulsion and pools.

questions.q: Why does redfish work in place of the classic sole?
questions.answer: Its firm, mild flesh holds together in the pan
distractors: It is an oily, rich fish that needs no sauce at all
It is a flat fish, just like sole
Its strong taste stands up to grapes
questions.why: Red drum is a firm, mild, slightly sweet round fish; it keeps its shape when cooked and leaves room for the grapes and the butter sauce.

questions.q: By tradition, what is Sole Véronique named after?
questions.answer: An operetta by André Messager
distractors: A grape grown in the Loire
The Paris hotel that served it first
A saint's day in the French calendar
questions.why: Tradition names the dish for Messager's operetta, first staged in Paris in 1898, and credits it to Escoffier; tell it as a story, since tellings vary.

questions.q: A guest asks whether the redfish is wild Louisiana catch. What is the honest answer?
questions.answer: I will ask the chef where ours comes from
distractors: Yes, caught off Grand Isle this morning
Yes, all our fish is wild Louisiana
No, redfish only lives in Texas
questions.why: Louisiana has had no commercial redfish fishery since the late 1980s; ours is farmed or legally caught elsewhere, and the chef knows which.

questions.q: To what internal temperature does FDA guidance cook a fish fillet?
questions.why: FDA guidance cooks fish to 63°C (145°F), when the flesh is opaque and flakes; poultry, not fish, is the 74°C (165°F) figure.

entries.title: Pecan Gulf Fish
entries.summary: A breakfast and lunch main course: the Gulf fish of the day topped with Louisiana lump crab, with a pecan bordelaise, cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens. Today's fish, which bordelaise, and every nut or shellfish question are settled with the kitchen.
entries.guest: Our Pecan Gulf Fish is today's local catch, topped with Louisiana lump crab, with a nutty pecan bordelaise, a silky cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens.

paras: The Pecan Gulf Fish is the Gulf fish plate of the breakfast and lunch menu: the day's catch topped with Louisiana lump crab, sauced with a pecan bordelaise and set over a cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens. It eats lighter than the egg dishes but still satisfies: nutty, buttery and sweet from the crab, with earthy greens.

Two things make it a Chef de Partie dish. The fish changes with what the boats bring, so it is learned at lineup, never guessed. And bordelaise means two different sauces: in a French kitchen a red wine sauce, in a New Orleans dining room usually a garlic butter. Which one the kitchen means changes the wine you pour.

Gulf fish means the day's catch, drum, sheepshead, snapper, grouper, triggerfish, speckled trout and others, from flaky to firm. A fillet is usually sautéed: a wide pan and a little fat hot before it goes in, the presentation side down first, left alone to colour, turned once and finished gently. Many kitchens dust it with flour first, the meunière way, for a golden crust. Thin fillets take 2 to 3 minutes in all, most of it on the first side; thick ones finish in the oven. FDA guidance cooks fish to 63°C (145°F), opaque and flaking. Our kitchen's preparation is learned at lineup.

Lump crab is the large, sweet body meat of the blue crab, sold already cooked, so it is only warmed, in a little butter or under the salamander, the kitchen's overhead grill; cooked again it turns stringy and loses its sweetness. Pecans toast quickly: spread on a tray in an oven at about 175°C (347°F) for 6 to 10 minutes, stirred once, until fragrant and a shade darker. A minute more and they turn bitter.

A New Orleans bordelaise is garlic and parsley in butter, often with olive oil, spooned hot over fish or bread; a pecan version works toasted pecans into it. The French bordelaise is another sauce entirely: red wine and shallot reduced with demi-glace, brown sauce reduced until glossy, and finished with bone marrow. A cauliflower purée is usually simmered in milk and cream and blended until velvety, lighter than potato, and collards wilted quickly keep a little chew.

New Orleans cooks have long put the pecan where French recipes put the almond. The praline became a pecan sweet, and fish à la meunière with almonds, amandine, found Louisiana cousins in pecan butter sauces and pecan-crusted fillets on menus across the city. The pecan is native to Louisiana and the Mississippi valley, rich, buttery and softer than an almond, which is why it melts so readily into a butter sauce.

This plate fails on timing. A pan not hot enough sticks and steams instead of colouring the fish, and a fillet left too long dries and falls apart. Lump crab cooked twice turns stringy, pecans a minute too long turn bitter, and garlic browned in butter held too hot turns acrid. A loose purée weeps water across the plate: cook it down.

On our plate the fish is the Gulf fish of the day, likely sautéed or pan-roasted to order, so know it and its preparation before service: every table will ask. The crab is Louisiana lump crab, warmed gently. The pecan bordelaise most likely belongs to the New Orleans garlic butter family, with toasted pecans worked into the butter, but that is a reading, not a recipe: confirm with the kitchen which bordelaise it is before pairing wine. Beneath sit the cauliflower purée and wilted collards, not the long-simmered Southern pot.

Offer it to a guest who wants fish at midday, something lighter than eggs, or the local catch: name today's fish first, then the crab. Do not confuse it with the Gulf Fish en Papillote at dinner, steamed in a banana leaf. This one plate carries fish, crab, pecans and very likely butter, so every allergen question, tree nuts and shellfish above all, goes to the service note and the kitchen before the order is placed. With a garlic butter bordelaise, a creamy, fresh Chardonnay suits; if today's sauce is red wine based, a light red Burgundy takes its place.

ratios.label: Toasting pecans
ratios.value: Oven at about 175°C (347°F), 6 to 10 minutes, stirred once

ratios.label: Thin fillet in the sauté pan
ratios.value: 2 to 3 minutes in all, most on the first side; thick fillets finish in the oven

faults.cause: Pan or fat not hot enough, or the fillet turned too soon.
faults.fix: Heat the pan first, lay the fillet away from you and wait until it releases before turning.

faults.cause: Lump crab cooked again instead of warmed.
faults.fix: Warm it gently in a little butter or under the salamander, just to heat.
Toast a fresh batch, watching closely; pull them at fragrant and a shade darker.

faults.cause: The garlic browned in butter held too hot.
faults.fix: Keep the butter warm, not frying; make a fresh batch if the garlic has coloured.

brennans.how: The fish is the day's Gulf catch, likely sautéed or pan-roasted to order; learn today's fish and its preparation at lineup, because every table will ask.
Most likely the New Orleans garlic butter family with toasted pecans, not the French red wine sauce; confirm with the kitchen which bordelaise it is before pairing wine.

A velvety cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens, which keep a little chew, sit beneath the fish: earthy, quiet partners for the crab and the pecan sauce.

cards.front: What is on the Pecan Gulf Fish plate?
cards.back: The Gulf fish of the day topped with Louisiana lump crab, a pecan bordelaise, cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens.

cards.front: What does Gulf fish mean on our menu?
cards.back: The day's catch, not one species: drum, sheepshead, snapper, trout and others. Learn today's fish and preparation at lineup.

cards.front: What are the two sauces called bordelaise?
cards.back: The French one is red wine and shallot reduced with demi-glace and bone marrow; in New Orleans it usually means garlic butter.

cards.front: Why confirm the bordelaise with the kitchen before pairing wine?
cards.back: A garlic butter calls for a creamy white such as Chardonnay; a red wine sauce calls for a light red, so the sauce decides the bottle.

cards.front: How is lump crab handled on the plate?
cards.back: It is already cooked, so it is only warmed gently; cooked again, it turns stringy and loses its sweetness.

cards.front: How is a fish fillet sautéed?
cards.back: In a little hot fat in a wide pan, presentation side first, left to colour, turned once and finished gently, in the oven if thick.

cards.front: How are pecans toasted, and what is the risk?
cards.back: In an oven at about 175°C (347°F) for 6 to 10 minutes, stirred once; a minute too long and they turn bitter.

cards.front: Why do pecans dress fish in New Orleans?
cards.back: Louisiana cooks put the native pecan where French recipes used almonds, so amandine has pecan cousins: pecan butter sauces and pecan-crusted fish.

cards.front: Which ingredients on this one plate must every guest hear about?
cards.back: Fish, crab, pecans and very likely butter: tree nut and shellfish questions go to the service note and the kitchen before ordering.

cards.front: How is the Pecan Gulf Fish told apart from the Gulf Fish en Papillote?
cards.back: The pecan fish is the breakfast and lunch plate, with a pecan bordelaise; the papillote is the dinner fish steamed in a banana leaf with olives and sorghum. Both carry crab and nuts, so send every allergen question to the kitchen.

cards.front: How do our collard greens differ from the Southern pot?
cards.back: They are wilted quickly and keep a little chew, not the long-simmered Southern pot; how they are seasoned is a question for the kitchen.

cards.front: When is a sautéed fillet done?
cards.back: At 63°C (145°F), when the flesh turns opaque and flakes at a touch; much past that it dries.

questions.q: In a New Orleans dining room, what does bordelaise usually mean?
questions.answer: A garlic butter, often with parsley
distractors: A red wine sauce with bone marrow
A tomato sauce with the trinity
A cream sauce with mushrooms
questions.why: The French bordelaise is red wine, shallot, demi-glace and marrow; in New Orleans the word usually names a garlic butter spooned over fish or bread.

questions.q: The kitchen says today's pecan bordelaise is the New Orleans garlic butter. Which wine style suits it?
questions.answer: A creamy, fresh Chardonnay
distractors: A big, tannic Cabernet Sauvignon
A sweet Mosel Auslese
A fortified Banyuls
questions.why: A garlic and pecan butter wants a white with texture and acidity, such as Chardonnay; were it the French red wine bordelaise, a light red Burgundy would take its place.

questions.q: Lump crab goes on the fish at the pass. How should it be handled?
questions.answer: Warmed gently, never recooked
distractors: Boiled for 10 minutes to cook it
Fried until crisp and golden
Served straight from the fridge
questions.why: Picked lump crab is sold cooked; warming keeps it sweet and whole, while cooking it again turns it stringy.

questions.q: A guest asks what the Gulf fish is today. What do you do?
questions.answer: Name the fish learned at lineup
distractors: Say it is always redfish
Guess from the menu description
Say the kitchen keeps it secret
questions.why: Gulf fish means the day's catch, not one species, so the server learns today's fish and its preparation at lineup and never guesses.

questions.q: Pecans for the sauce are toasting in a 175°C (347°F) oven. What is the main risk?
questions.answer: A minute too long and they turn bitter
distractors: They never colour at that heat
They soften and turn chewy
Their oil sets hard as they cool on the tray
questions.why: Rich in oil, pecans go from fragrant to burnt quickly; they come out at 6 to 10 minutes, a shade darker, and a bitter batch is toasted again.

questions.q: Pecans in a fish butter sauce are the Louisiana swap for which nut of the French kitchen?
questions.answer: Almonds
distractors: Walnuts
Hazelnuts
Pistachios
questions.why: Louisiana cooks put the native pecan where French recipes used almonds, so the logic of trout amandine carries over to pecan butter sauces.

questions.q: How should a fish fillet go into the sauté pan?
questions.answer: Presentation side down into hot fat
distractors: Into a cold pan, heated slowly
Turned every 30 seconds
Into deep oil until it floats to the top
questions.why: The first side into hot fat takes the best colour, so the side the guest sees goes down first; left alone it releases, is turned once and finished gently.

questions.q: The dish's name says pecan and Gulf fish. Which ingredient on the plate does the name leave out, though every guest must hear about it?
questions.answer: The Louisiana lump crab
distractors: The cauliflower purée
The wilted collard greens
The toasted pecans
questions.why: The name says pecan and fish, but lump crab crowns the plate; name the crab, the pecans and the fish, and send every allergen question to the service note and the kitchen.

questions.q: How is the Pecan Gulf Fish told apart from the Gulf Fish en Papillote?
questions.answer: The daytime plate, with a pecan bordelaise
distractors: The dinner plate, steamed in a banana leaf
The dinner plate, with olives and sorghum
A breakfast fish under hollandaise
questions.why: The pecan fish is the breakfast and lunch plate with a pecan bordelaise; the papillote is the dinner fish steamed in a banana leaf with olives and sorghum. Both carry crab.
